newsitem.title: USA: Prices up in 12th district urban areas -- S.F. Fed.
newsitem.headline: Prices up in 12th district urban areas -- S.F. Fed.

text.p: Inflation picked up substantially in major urban areas in the 12th U.S. economic district in 1996 and early 1997 as prolonged tight labor markets triggered wage and price increases, an official at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco said.
And there is a good chance that wage-driven inflation may spread throughout the region, he added.
"If you look at the inflation performance, at least in major cities in the West, we are seeing an increase in inflation," Robert Valletta, an economist at the San Francisco Fed, told Reuters.
"And there is a very good chance that that will spread throughout the 12th district and probably mirror developments occurring in other parts of the country," he added.
Valletta said the major urban areas he was referring to include the San Francisco Bay area, the Seattle area, the Portland, Oregon area and also Las Vegas and Salt Lake City.

"Because the areas I've just mentioned have had such tight labor markets for such a long time now, for at least a few years, we have seen wage inflation and price inflation increasing in those areas," Valletta said.
"And those sorts of dense urban areas probably tend to lead the rest of the nation in inflation," the San Francisco Fed economist added.

Valletta added that inflation numbers for the region as a whole are still subdued, "but that doesn't necessarily mean that that won't change in either the short or slightly longer run." He also said that he has not detected broad-based wage pressures for the region as a whole either.
The 12th district encompasses Alaska, Arizona, California, Hawaii, Nevada, Idaho, Utah and Washington, plus Guam, American Samoa and the northern Mariana Islands.

The San Francisco Fed economist also said the 12th district economy continues to grow at a very fast clip, adding that he expected job growth in the region to stay at around an annualized 3.5 percent rate in the third quarter.
"The economy is running at a very rapid rate these days.
"Job growth in the region has been running on an annual basis just below 3.5 percent over the last year and a half, and I see no reason why that won't continue in the third quarter," Valletta said.
The San Francisco Fed economist said the production sector has been the driving force of the region's economy.
The manufacturing area, both durables and non-durables, coupled with construction have been the flagships of the region's long-lasting economic expansion, he added.
"I think the production end of things is where all the action is these days," Valletta said.
Despite the strong industrial activity in the region, Valletta said consumer spending has been solid but not extraordinary.
"Consumer spending is okay. I woudn't describe consumer spending as pretty strong ... Solid would be a more accurate reflection," he said.
The San Francisco Fed economist added that consumer spending in the region has not been as strong as some analysts might have expected.
Valletta also said the positive growth seen in the region has contributed to improved fiscal health of the states in the 12th district.
"On the whole, the very strong fiscal position of the states reflect strong economic conditions and is likely to reinforce those strong conditions assuming that the money is spent wisely," he said.
Valletta did not discuss the current level of interest rates or the future of the Fed's monetary policy.

The Fed's policy setting committee will meet next on August 19 to deliberate on interest rates. The Fed last changed policy on March 25, when it raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to the current 5.50 percent.
The central bank kept policy unchanged in the May and July meetings of its Federal Open Market Committee.
Many pundits and Fed watchers on Wall Street expect the Fed to keep monetary policy unchanged during its next meeting in August.
